line: Good evening. Vasant Deshpande, I'm the president of the association. You are new here?
choice1: Yes. I'm {playerName}. I just moved in.

line: Good evening. Vasant Deshpande. I keep the roof fund and the language school. For everything else there is Meena; she runs the association now. You are new here?
choice1: Yes. I'm {playerName}. I just moved in.

line: Welcome. If you need the washroom, it is past the stage, on the left. The light switch is outside the door, which is a design error.
No. I was a civil engineer for the county for thirty years, so I notice these things. This building was a carpet warehouse until 1998.
We bought it. Two hundred and twelve families, with our own money. No bank would lend to an association with no history, so we raised it in fourteen months.
It was arithmetic, mostly. Ten dollars a month from each family. Some gave more and told nobody. I know who. I don't say.
Not one. I know what a grant looks like. Ten pages of money, forty pages of conditions.
Reports. Programs they choose, hours they choose. And when the money stops, the city's people stop coming. $ The families stay. That is what I have seen, three times now.
choice1: So the hall runs on families?

line: The Sunday language school, the roof fund, the Diwali program. All families. My grandchildren will need somewhere to come back to.
choice1: I'd like to help keep it.
choice2: Good to meet you, Mr. Deshpande.

line: Riverside Park. Doctor's orders: thirty minutes, brisk. I measured the loop myself. It is 1.3 kilometres.
choice3: I should let you sit down.

line: It's adequate. The sign says one mile. A mile is 1.61 kilometres. Somebody at the city cannot convert.
Twice, in writing. I was with the county thirty years, I know which desk to write to. They thanked me. The sign is still there.
choice1: What did you do for the county?

line: Bridges and drainage. Not glamorous. Now I have the hall's drainage, which is worse. If you walk there in the evening, you will see me on my second lap.
choice1: Maybe I'll walk it with you.

line: Good evening. I've come straight from my walk in the park. _looks at his watch_ Fourteen minutes, twelve seconds, the first lap. I write it down.
choice2: How many laps do you do?

line: Three. Thirty-nine minutes, if I'm honest with the watch. The doctor said thirty. I give him nine extra, free.
Since I retired. Before that I walked from the parking lot to my desk. Seventy metres. Now I walk the park, and then I come here and sit on a folding chair.
choice1: What do you think about while you walk?

line: The roof, mostly. And the language school. Forty-one children on Sundays now. Twelve years ago we had ninety.
Soccer. Swimming. Sunday is a busy day for an American child. _is quiet for a moment_ The parents still sign them up. Then the soccer schedule comes out.
choice1: Could you move it to Saturday?
choice3: I'm sorry. I'll let you rest.

line: Then it would be Saturday soccer. I have done the arithmetic. _writes the lap time in a small notebook_ Tomorrow, three laps again.
choice1: I'll walk one with you sometime.

line: Good morning. You're early. I'm early because the roofer is late.
He said eight. It is eight forty. He is bringing me a new quote, which I already know will be wrong.
The roof needs nine thousand dollars before winter. We have six. He will say eleven, and I will show him his own quote from March.
choice1: How do you raise the other three?

line: Three hundred families giving ten dollars. It's arithmetic. The hard part is the three hundred, not the ten.
Two hundred and six, so far. The ones who don't, I don't ask twice. They come for Diwali, and they look at the ceiling.
Thank you. That makes two hundred and seven. The box is by the door. I write a receipt for every gift, even ten.
Good morning. You are punctual. The board meets at nine; it is eight fifty-two.
choice3: I'll get out of the way.

line: I chair it. Thirty-one items on the agenda. I wrote twenty-nine of them. The other two are Meena's.
The library would like to borrow our chairs, and the clinic would like the hall on a Monday. Both very kind. $ In my experience, when the city borrows something, it comes back with a form attached.

I say we discuss it, which is a slower no. $ [neutral] Sit in, if you like. Visitors may not vote, but they may listen. In five years someone your age will have to chair this, and at present nobody your age has read an agenda.
Good morning. You are early. Meena is not here yet, and she has the agenda.
She chairs the board now. I proposed her myself, three years ago. I wanted somebody who would answer the telephone.

I do the roof and the numbers. That is the part that falls down if nobody does it. She does the people. She has more of them than I do. $ Last month she brought the library people to see our kitchen. They took photographs.

They will come once. The families come every week. I tell her this, and she says, then the families will meet them. _straightens the chairs at the table_ Perhaps. Come on Sundays, at least. The language school needs grown-ups, not visitors.
Ah, {playerName}. Good. Have you a minute? I have a question for you.
The young ones come for Diwali and the food. You come on a Tuesday. Why?
Good answers, both of them. You have a good head. I wish you were here more.
choice1: Why does it matter so much?

line: The young ones think the hall will always be here. Halls stay because someone stays late and locks up. I have locked this door about four thousand times.
choice2: People stay late in other places too.

line: They do. I'm not against other places. I would only like to know who will lock this one when I can't. At present, nobody.
Ah, good. Sunday evening. Are you free?
The building committee has dinner at my home. Six people, seven with you. My wife is making puran poli.
The committee needs someone under sixty. At present the youngest member is sixty-three. Also, you listen when I read out numbers.
Good afternoon. You've seen the news, I expect.
Three families called the hall this morning. They wanted the lawyer's number.
choice2: Did you have one to give?

line: On retainer, since 2003. Four hundred dollars a year, from the general fund. People laughed at me for it.
choice3: I'll let you take your calls.

line: Because Washington changes its mind. A program can close. The association has a phone number nobody can take away. $ [neutral] Today, eleven calls.
choice1: What does the lawyer tell them?
choice2: We can't do everything alone, though.

line: What their papers say, and what they don't. He is not a miracle, but he answers on a Sunday. $ People ask me if I am surprised by all this. I am not. Some years this country says what it thinks of us quietly, some years loudly.
Good afternoon. Everyone is talking about the new president.
I read the speech. Twice. It was a good speech.
choice2: What did you like about it?

line: The hall has seen six presidents. The roof leaked under all six. $ This one noticed us because four hundred families in this county registered and voted together, and three vans drove the aunties to the polls. Nobody gave us that speech. We earned it.
Votes and patience. Now there is a new grant for community centres, Meena tells me. Forty pages. She would like us to apply.

I said I would read it. I have read eleven pages. On page nine they want to approve our programming. $ Our own people organised and put that president in office. A grant with forty pages of conditions is how the power goes back to the city.
choice1: Keep reading. Maybe it gets better.

line: Good evening. You are here so often I have added you to the roof fund spreadsheet.
As a volunteer. Not a donor, don't worry. Column F.
choice1: Put me down for the ladder.

line: Names and hours. Suresh Nair, eleven hours. Karthik, four, all at the sound board. You, zero, for now.
Because in 1998 we did everything with hours, not money. Every tile of that floor, somebody laid on a Saturday. I have the list somewhere, in pencil.
It's in the office, in a binder marked 1998, next to the deed. When the young ones say we should take city money, I show them the binder. Most of them stop talking.
choice1: I'd like to see it sometime.

line: Ah. I haven't seen you here for a while. Meena says the library.
choice2: I still come here, Mr. Deshpande.

line: Very busy, I'm sure. I hope the library also needs someone on a ladder.
To return my wife's books. Seven days late, usually. The fine is twenty-five cents a day. I pay it exactly.
It's a good place. It's not ours. That's not a complaint. When the city closes that branch on Sundays, which it will, this hall will still be open.
Hm. You came back.
choice1: I spoke out of turn before. I'm sorry.

line: Accepted. One apology is sufficient. People who apologise three times usually want something.
Not now, I'm checking the roof quote against the last one. They've made an error. In their favour, naturally.
